blocks.x: First thing we usually ask is your full name.
Well, my full name is Emanuel Renne Sales.
How do you spell Emanuel?
Emanuel, E-M-A-N-U-E-L.
And Renne?
Renne with R-E-N-E and a little dash on top of the E.
That's an acute.
And then Sales, S-A-Y-L-E-S, but it's pronounced like S-A-L-E-S.
I see. Is that why I can't find you in the phone book?

Well, no, we're listed in the phone book, not the manual cell. We're listed under my deceased father George's cell. Oh, I see. And I have a brother, Joe's cell, who's listed in the phone book, but he lives up on Franklin Street. He don't play music, he's a painter by Trey. And I have another brother, George's cell, but he's listed under his wife, Maiden, who lives on St. Anthony, and he lives right next door to Paul Barberand.
Oh, yeah.
Yeah, 2607, I believe that's a good scene.
Well, let's go back before your time, back as far as we can, I guess. You say your father played?

Yeah, my father was one of the original men of what they call the Silver Leaf Band. It was a string band. And from what he told me, there was a man that played violin. See the name of the iPhone's? They were out in the riverfront. He played violin and sax. Do you remember him? No, I don't get it. And then he and my daddy and there was, my daddy played guitar and he on violin. And then they had a bass. And I don't remember what a bass player, but at that time, my daddy tell me they used to, all the fellas used to work in a deal, like poor jobs, different jobs, because the fellas was getting in time. And then on the weekends, they'd always go around and serenade, like for instance, I remember you always tell me about like St. Charles Street. They'd go around, had different people that'd go around and serenade and pick up money. And then they'd come down the Irish Channel. My daddy was born and raised out there in the Irish Channel. In fact, he had some cousins that still lives on Phillip Street. That's about between Annunciation and Laura or something like that. And from when I was told, the house that they lived in was the house that my daddy's mother and father once owned. Then there was another house that he had one time that he owned, but he lost that to his half-sister one time. And then after, when he got mad, he always said, well, the children started coming so fast, he had to give up music, so he had to go get him a job. So with the Stella and all, he would play at some time on weekends, and he always told me how he met my mother. My mother's originally from Donaldsonville, Louisiana. Well, Donaldsonville, Louisiana is the home of the Claiborne. That was one of the great teacher and brass band, dance band. They had for Louisiana. And I remember a kid very well. Where we lived on the street was about a half a block from one of the man's street called a railroad. Then they had a school, and in the back of the school was a square. And in the back of that was the courthouse. And in that square, they had what they call a pavilion. I remember every Sunday, this band, Claiborne band, seemed like it was hired through the city to play a concert. And they had whites in the color all around in the park. We'd listen to that, and the band was dressed up in very nice uniform. They looked very nice, and it was built in a circle like, you know. And the leader, Claiborne would be up in the center directing, you know, the band with his baton and everything. They played, well, they did mostly reading. Everything was read, and they played marches and a lot of pop tunes that were popular at that time for brass bands, see.
Does that look familiar, Donaldsonville Railroad Avenue?
Well, no, this is, yeah, yeah, I can see a little resembling here. Seemingly this is about near about the, yeah, that's the station here. I can see that.
Remember the market or the opera house?
Yeah, yeah, I remember this, this, yeah, the market. This was the market, yeah. This was going the opposite towards by the river. Let's see, this.
Bank of Ascension.
Yeah, Bank of Ascension.
Remember that?
Yeah, this, this, this, yeah, this picture here. You know what I'm building? Let's see, this.
There's Railroad Avenue.
Yeah, Bank of Ascension, yeah, yeah.
Remember that street?

Oh, yeah, oh, yeah. Uh-huh. This look like round about the, either it was a theater or a hotel, yeah. It looks more like it was a theater. Now, what I'm building, yeah, Railroad Avenue, yeah. Now, it's a funny thing to remember the streets, the cross streets.
Yeah, it looks like, yeah. Humus, how do you say that? H-O-U, Homus Street or something?
Homus Street, yeah. A whole lot of this, yeah, I can see this, yeah, one of the, where I find the neighborhood. There's the whole town out there.
Oh, yeah. Mm-hmm.
Yeah, I can remember this. Mississippi Street, did you ever? Yeah, I remember that, I remember that street, yeah.
Yeah. Uh-huh.

Uh-huh. And I remember the street that we lived on was the head of running, go to railroad street, which is about half a block. There was a store named Babin, B-A-U-B-I-N, we used to trade from. And, uh, I went to a public school going towards railroad street, going towards, from my house, to the railroad station. But, uh, my first school was through a, a colored lady named Miss, uh, Rita. Mm-hmm. So I was a little private, a primary school, you know, where you go and learn your APCs and everything. And from there I went to this public school. They had a, a Catholic school there for, for the colored term, but, I mean, my people didn't send me there. They sent me to this school. And eventually we left, uh, we moved out of Donaldsonville around, I'd say about 1915. Uh-huh. And, uh, my father, the reason for the family was in, uh, Donaldsonville because that was my mother's home, and she had a home there with my grandfather. And the thing was kind of tough, and my dad, my dad would go in the city and find work, see, because he couldn't find work around Donaldsonville so much, see. And finally I remember he did come to Donaldsonville and they got him a job at, uh, the hotel. I think it was Hotel Donaldsonville, one of the biggest hotels they had there. And I remember, well, my dad used to sometime play a game. They had another band. Uh, uh, it was from out, uh, had a place called Frogamore. That was on the other side of the railroad track in Donaldsonville. Well, uh, Clayborne was a D-Light band, you see. And my daddy could play with them, but they was already, they already had the number of men that they needed, you see. But they knew all of them, and sometimes he'd go play with the Sunderband, and they used to kid him by playing with the Trashy Band. But that was, you know, they had to make a little money, you see. And then one time I remember he worked on, um, like a hauling, uh, in the railroad station, uh, fooling with trunks and things. Because I remember my mother used to have to rub his back when he'd come home and he had to quit that job, because it was too hard for him. But he finally got a job in, uh, in the hotel where he was sort of, uh, pulled in a night desk man, you know. Oh, I see. He used to come around and tell us kids where he tells about his particular night's work, you know, and everything. And that's how he'd become the new, a lot of the nice and rich white people around Donaldsonville, you see.
By the way, uh, did you ever know where Joe Oliver was from?

My daddy knew Joe Oliver very well. He used to always tell me about Joe Oliver, how he was, uh, he used to eat so much, and how he was bragging on how much coffee and things he could drink always more than anybody. And, uh, I remember one time that he told me he was staying on 4th Street. And that was about around 1915, because my daddy used to always talk to me about, because it looked like he thought I had an inclination for music, playing music, you see. And he was a guitar player, you see. And, uh, he used to tell me about Joe Oliver, how he could play and how he could, uh, hold a note and how he worked on the riverfront. That's what it was, you see. Joe Oliver worked on the riverfront and used to take his horn and go down. And then he'd never remember anything he told me about a place on a magazine, I believe it was Magazine Authority, these white people that Joe Oliver worked for. And that's how he brought his first, uh, what they call him, cornette in those days. And the white people used to let him go out on the weekends and play, but he had to come back to come to work that Monday morning, see. And, uh.
You say he worked on the riverfront, was he a longshoreman?
I said I think so at that time.
And he take his cornette down with him?

Well, maybe he did, but I know he did that, because you know guys had to find some kind of way of making money, because music was, you know, just like his job. You know, on the weekend you get like that. And then I remember he told me strictly about this place, and I think it was his magazine, it might have been 30 magazines, some people he worked for. And they would have, you know, saw that he had a job, and then let him go out and play, you know, to keep up with his home, you see. And that's, uh, that's where the story is, as far as I can remember. And then one time, I remember, like I said, he stayed on Fort Street. I don't know whether it was Fort out there by the, what they call Irish Channel 2, see, because Fort runs all the way out that way. Yeah.
Well, Joe Oliver was here in the city when he was a young boy then.
Oh yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah.
I wondered if he was from the country originally?

Well, I'm mad because from what my, my dad remembers, quite a fellow's, a musician that came here, from different parts of, out of New Orleans. See, they would, they would hear about New Orleans, and they'd probably, in fact, I remember dad used to tell me about, uh, old man, Ompren, the fathers are the one now. Mm-hmm. Said he used to go out in those countries and teach.
Mm-hmm.

And he used to, uh, make his money by paying him somebody for teaching and selling them instruments and writing their, their music. You know, instructing their music for them and teach the brass band and instruct them private and everything. Said he made a lot of his money that way. And that's how I imagine a lot of the fellas after they learned and everything and they heard somebody talk about New Orleans after they learned how to play, they'd want to come to New Orleans and, and, and get work, see? And find a way, cause I remember like, uh, uh, uh, Bebe Rizzling. My dad, I remember when he first come here. And, uh, cause he was from on, uh, like on the outskirt. And then another man, John Robich, with a left hand violin player, he used to play in the lyrics theater. My dad used to keep him by then. He said he came to New Orleans playing an accordion. I remember the little, they call him a, a wind jammer. Wind jammer. I think it's a wind jammer or something. Yeah. He said he brought him up to see Dave Perkin. He said Dave Perkin laughed at him. He said, man, you can't make no money with that. He got, you got to play some kind of instrument. So I don't know how he, well, he learned violin when he came here, but I knew he was, he, he was a violin player. And my daddy played with him quite a bit. And then there was, uh, another fellow. He was, uh, responsible of, of having, uh, what they call, uh, one of the, uh, famous Negro, uh, uh, uh, uh, uh, club, uh, uh, uh, let's see what you call that. Society. In other words, he came here as a, as a waiter. And he got with the rich, good, rich people. And through being a waiter, through John Robichaud, he got the job for the musician. So that's how John got his start. And today is, is, uh, it's, it's a club now, young man twenties, I believe. And this man used to, used to have, uh, little things on weekends for the people that wanted to learn how to dance. All the colored people wanted to learn how to dance. And, uh, they would have their things in any form of clubs. And that's responsible of, of the, of the young, I think it's the young man twenties. One of those big colored things we have right now. That's how they started. And, uh, what we're going back to, uh, to, uh, John, uh, yeah, John Robichaud. Yeah. How he came here. And, uh, there's another fellow. He didn't even know how, when, when Celestan came here from out of the country. Where did he come from? Well, I can't think exactly right now, what time, but I know he remember when he, when he first came here.
Somebody mentioned that Froggy Moore once, that he was up there. What was that little suburb, little town, village? Froggy Moore.
I remember there was a place called, like I said, from Donnellsville, where they called Froggy Moore from Donnellsville.
Well, Richard M. Jones was from around that neighborhood too, I think. Yeah. Did you ever know him? He was a piano player?

Richard John. I heard him. Miney, they called him. Miney, yeah, yeah, yeah. Well, he's, I think he's the way or could avoid me, but I heard him talk about it. Now, there's another fellow that I remember, since we were speaking about that, uh, I met, he, uh, he, uh, he, uh, like the late John Porter. He come from around, around Lecce, and also he had a pal of his, uh, David John. They came from out around that section, see? Sure. Like I said, like a lot of those fellows, they, they came here and they, like I said, one of those professors like Willie Humpin, and, and, and, you know, I think Mr. Porkin did quite a little teaching, because he taught white and colored. Uh-huh. Because he was very fair, he looked like the white, a lot of people thought he was white, see? But he was a very close, from my dad, a friend, from, my dad, from way out, uh, when out in Irish Channel. A lot of the fellows like, like, like King, the late Kimball father, my daddy knew him well. There was another fellow named, I believe it was Jim Johnson, played bass violin. My daddy knew him well. Mm-hmm. And, um, another fellow, Steve Lewis, and what my dad, my mother told me, of course he's very young than my daddy, but I mean, my, my father told me that my mother's sister, Aunt Bella, that, that was, uh, Steve in the name. In other words, she christened him. Yeah. In the early years, when I did have a chance to play with Steve, he told me the same thing. He said, yeah, that's, that's my name.
Aunt Bella, she's?

My, my, my, my mother's sister, which is my auntie. We call, we call Aunt Bella. What is that name? Uh-huh. Well, she married her, my, my, my, my maiden name was Latoya, like my mother, but she married a Raphael. That's Peter, that's Peter, that's Peter Raphael's mother. You know, you know, Peter Raphael played drums. Got his lady cut off now. Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. Oh, that's my first cousin. Yeah?
Yeah. Did we get your father's name? I don't know that you gave his name.
My father's name was Joy Sails.
Mm-hmm. You know, um, when he was born, or can you tell us about when he died?

Well, let's see, now, my father died, jealousy, 1910. And he was seven to nine, I remember well. Seven to nine. I saw him, on the tombstone. Yeah, yeah, yeah. My father was about seven to nine, yeah. And he died then. Is he buried, uh, back in St. Louis, number two? No, he's buried in, uh, I can't get that cemetery. I think there's, it's back there on City Park, where that Higgin, used to be the Higgin Plain. Hope Cemetery.
Hope Cemetery. Hope Cemetery. Yeah.

My sister, my mother, and my father are buried back there. Yeah. Yeah. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Now, let's see, we were back to, uh, to the time of, uh, when Donisonville. Mm-hmm. Well, I didn't get to the time when, uh, when we left, I said we left Donisonville by 1915. And I was telling you about the, uh, Claiborne Williams Band, how they were the predominant fact and truth. I don't remember any, not a fireman, I believe, had a band. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.

Yeah. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . And Claiborne, I would say, was like when I came to New Orleans, like Dave Poikin was. He taught both white and colored. Because I remember there was a white student and he had to go to their house and teach them, you see. And he was very known, I mean, as a very good teacher because there were many good musicians that came in colored and white that came to be a good musician that he had actually started. Now he was another one that used to go away with the shows and things. And he had a brother, which my father always told me, that played trombone. My father always put it this way because my father always used to listen to the famous band. I remember his famous band was like Wayne King and Guy Lombardo and this other fellow that played the trombone, Tommy Dawson. He said every time he heard Tommy Dawson, it reminded me of Claiborne's brother, George. Now George, he told me, was what you call an adventure fellow. He always did travel with shows. He never stayed around Donaldsonville so very much. He'd come back when the season would be over and say most of the time he'd come back, he'd be sick. And my father told me this story about George William that the last time he came back there, he was very sick. But it seemed like it must have been a cold, must have had a very bad case of pneumonia. Anyhow, there was some kind of medicine they had. The doctor had to send over to France to get, to rub him with. And he said his own brother, Claiborne William, nobody else didn't want to rub him because he was afraid they would, you know. My father said he was the one that went over there and volunteered to rub him down and put this particular salve on because the doctors there had recommended this was the only thing that was going to do him any good. But he finally died from the stir the way my father told me about it and he was a very close friend to the family of my mother and him. He knew my mother's sisters and brothers and all of them and my grandfather and all of them because if I can recall a block, we didn't live but two half a block from the Claiborne on the same street. But it was going the opposite direction from the railroad which I remember was going back to the graveyard because I have a sister that was her pirate and we used to call him Mr. Tellers for, he was the one that took care of the graveyard back up there. And the family on the other side, they still have a tomb there.
What about the funerals out there? Are they similar to the funerals here with brass bands?

Well, yes. Raybone had one of the famous brass bands. They'd had, like we had in New Orleans, I mean like when they'd have a funeral, the brass band would play. Now they didn't have so much second line like we had. They had some of it and then they would play a kind of jazz tune coming back, you see. But I wouldn't say it was glamorous as New Orleans was, you know. They didn't do it that way so much. And then I remember when I was a kid and I think it was the Baptist and Methodist they used to have where they'd be going to the river for baptism. And you could hear a man humming for the start, seemingly it starts some way out from the program, about the tracks. And you could hear that big gathering in the street humming and singing if you're going to the river, you see. Yeah. And that was something I'd always picture as a kid. I remember well, I said it and it always had that rhythm and beat to the songs, you know. Everybody would be shouting and praying on the way and everything. And what I want to say, we moved out of Downsville, I'd say about 1915. And we moved up on Boedate and Oak, Boedate and Oak I remember very well. I was seemingly, I must have been about seven or eight years old then.
Just to check the dates on the thing now, when were you born?

I was born in 1907, January the 31st. And I was Christian there at the colored, I mean they didn't have any colored Catholic church in Downsville there, but I can't think of the name of the church, but it was a big Catholic church they had. And at that time the colored and white went to the same church, you know, what's the color that's in the back view, you know. Does this look like it?
Do you remember it says interior? Oh yeah, that's the church.

Yeah, that's the big church. It was about two blocks from the river. Yeah, that's it. That was a big, in other words, it looked just like this church on Tulane, that big Catholic church on Tulane, right past the child's hospital.
Is that it?
Oh yeah, yeah. I was looking at it, I was trying to wonder what this high steeple was. Yeah, this is the steeple of it, yeah.
You need a glass there, a magnifying glass.

And this facing this way is what you call facing the river, this way. Mm-hmm. Yeah. I can't think of the... You were born in Downsville in New Orleans? Yeah. No, I was born in Downsville. I should explain the reason for that.
Oh.
Oh. Mm-hmm.
I can't see it.
Can you see it? Yeah.
Yeah.
I can see it without the glass. Mm-hmm. Yeah. Old and New Catholic Church, it says. You need to broke the glass. What is it again? I can't see it. Old and New Catholic Church.
Church, yeah.
They need two different eyes.

Well, that's... They have a colored Catholic Church there now. Mm-hmm. I mean, well, it's been out since about around 30, I think. Mm-hmm. Yeah. Now, we'll see. I didn't get back to tell you, but I was...
Now, I was going to ask you about dates now. Where were you when the big storm was? Were you in the city? Are we out of there?

No, that big storm, I remember my grandfather was living. And I don't know whether he was here, but he had came to New Orleans after the storm. And he had... You know, my grandfather never did like New Orleans. I don't know why. And he had went down to the... I remember he was describing to the other sisters and brothers about how the French market was all... The top and thing was all tore down and everything. And my Aunt Bella was living here then, I'm sure, yeah. And he had another son. This is my Uncle Roscoe, yeah. And another son from my Uncle Thetto. I remember we're living here in New Orleans. And my Aunt Bridget was living here. My Aunt Maggie was living in here. And my great auntie, that would be my mother's sister, Big Nenang. She was a very dark woman with very cold, black hands. She could read and write French. Because I never did learn it. But I mean, from a kid I never did like French or Creole. But I mean, my sister, she had a chance to... I mean, not Creole, French. And it was told to me that she either went to France or she was instructed by some white people that taught her. Because she was, it seems, by trade. She was what you call a old-made woman that never got married. And she made her living by sewing. She was a very good sewer. And she could... She spoke very bad English. But anything in real... And she didn't understand Creole so much. I mean, but if you spoke real French, she could really understand. She could write French. She could write it, yeah. Yeah. Now let's say we were...
Just getting back to the city. Yeah.
Now I say we moved here. We left down to, I say, about 1915. I remember.
And the storm was in 1915.

Well, it might have been maybe not. I know I was in Donsonville when that storm was. I was... Maybe I might have been 1916. And I did remember we had a severe... We had a heavy snow. We were living in Donsonville. And I got to check on a year with that. What is that, 1916? Because I know right... It was shortly after that. And my father's family came, got a good job in Yarlene. And he moved us all to family. My mother and my sisters and brothers. My father was still living in Yarlene. I mean, he was here already. I mean, we moved everything to... And we lived up on the corner of Oak and Woodhead. And that's where I... Yeah, I went to where I left off. I went to a school called... They call it... It's called St. John of Arts now. But it was called St. Dominic at that time. And there's some particular corner. Like I said, I must have been about eight or nine years old. I remember when on Sunday, especially when the band would go around advertising for the dance that night. They had a saloon right across the street from us on the corner. That was where all the bands would stop and play the advertising. And then they would go in there and the fellow running the place would give them a little drink or refresh them, you know. And see when they were still in that particular corner long, you know. And from that time I always had... Well, I always had... Well, I was inclined from usually from Donovan listening to the Claiborne Williams Band in Donovan Village. And my dad was playing the guitar, you know, and everything. And my dad, I was told, played a little bass. And he also played a viola. And I was told, I used to be picking on a... I used to get me a piece of tin and a stick and used to be beat. And my mother was saying, she sure wish I learned how to play something. So we... So like I said, I've never taken the air and I always got an enthused about jazz and everything, you know. And about the bands in New Orleans. You can cut it.
That's all right. Keep on going. Yeah.

New Orleans. And I always said that I would want to be... I thought to myself, I'd want to be a musician to play in a jazz band. I had because the rhythm of the band and the way the guys played, it really was different from listening to bass bands, brass bands in New Orleans. And of course, Claiborne had an orchestra band, but...
It was different from what now?

From listening to brass bands in Donovanville, you know. Oh, I see. Because they were strictly readers, you know. But Claiborne Williams did have an orchestra band, but I mean, by me being a kid, I didn't really get a chance to go out there then, you see. Yeah. Yeah. So we... She lived up there on Birdhead and Oak. Like I said, all the bands used to stop there. And I don't know, I forgot the time behind there. We moved on Ramport Street between 6th and Washington. And I went to a school called the Holy Ghost School, which is still up there. And I remember one time, my daddy took the streets, my oldest brother Pete, and my next brother Joe. And before I get to that, he used to always find me plucking around with his guitar. You know, he had his guitar he kept there, and I'd be fooling around like a kid, and I couldn't make a card. I'd just be strumming and trying to find a note, you know. So I remember he took one day, he took my oldest brother Pete, and my brother Joe and myself, he said, I'm going to show you all a card. He said, I want you to see who's going to grasp the idea the fastest. So he'd show them a card, and then he'd give it to Pete, then he'd give it to Joe, and then he'd give it to me. And I'd take the card, and then he'd bring it back to them, and he found out that they couldn't catch the eye of holding the card. But I could, it seemed like I could remember what he showed me, see. And he took another card and showed them. Well, it seemed like he was testing to see which one would really want to learn how to play music, you see. So then he taught me, I remember, after he taught me how to play three changes, I remember in the key of G. That was the G chord, the D7, and the C chord. Then he took me to the key of C, and he taught me the C chord, the F, and the G7, those simple changes. And after I learned that, he saw why I could play that pretty well. And I remember there was a song out at that time called Go Feather Your Nest. And he showed me how to play the chords on that. So I said, well, he said, well, it looked like he said, but I don't want you to play no guitar. He said, I want you to play violin. So I said, okay, Paul, I think I learned that. So he said, I've already talked to Dave Poick, and he says, he's willing to take it. He said, I wouldn't want nobody else to teach you but him, because we were good friends from way back. He says, I want him to teach you. He said, now, you already, which I did already have my little job. I used to work, and I remember I was waking, but 75 cents a week. I was waking on Coliseum at 7. Yeah, Coliseum at 7. I was waking after school, going up there doing yard boy, and cleaning up the yard in the evening. And then I'd do the little butler work, serve the people, you know, and then help the cook, clean up the kitchen, and come on back. I'd get back about 7 or 8 o'clock at night and study my lesson and then go to base, you know. Well, after that, well, when he took me to Dave Poick, well, he had a fellow, my dad was working at the Masonic Temple, the old Masonic Temple, and the fellow down there,
seemed like he had this all playing out, what he wanted me to play.

White Father had a violin he'd been talking to that one, and after he finally talked to this man that he had a son that wanted to learn violin, but he didn't have no big money to pay for no violin, but he wanted to get a good violin. So this white gentleman must have told him about he has a violin there, and he would sell it to read him a price. And I think my dad had bought that violin for $10, and it was a real good violin. I think that violin must have worth about $50 at that time. And, you know, I should be fooled with that. I was running on my dad, he had a viola, that's what it was. A viola was just larger than a violin. That's what I took lesson on that from Dave Poick.
About how old were you? Can we get that?

Well, it's kind of hard. I should have figured it out, but I was in about fourth or fifth grade. Well, you're quite young. At that time, kids were pretty old. I mean, not like now, you know, so I must have been around about 10 or 11 years old, maybe older than that. Because I can wait and bring in this park.
