So, uh, we stayed around there, I'd say, uh... Oh, let's see. I came back here, it was just before 27. Uh-huh. Well, the band made a big hit. Uh-huh. And we didn't have no particular man, we had this particular man, Aaron Long, I forgot to tell you. He booked us on a trip, he gave up his market, and booked us on a trip from Pensacola to Jacksonville. And the fellow, George Morris, we were not talking to Aaron Long, talking to the band members, he said, if we get to Jacksonville, he said, I know if we get down to Tampa and Panama for all, he said, we'd make some money. He said, I was down there as a cook. And he said, they don't have no New Orleans Tampa band down there. He said, we know what we did in this territory. So, we played this guy here along, he was, I think a Mason or something like that, he knew it was a different thing, we played, oh, I remember we played Tallahassee, I remember that, but we played other places on the way going to Jacksonville. And we didn't have too much hardship in the city of the band, because we always had a place to eat, sleep, and sometimes the money was short, sometimes, but it was always a proposition. We made, we got good, it was on a, what you call a percentage proposition, you see. So when we got to Jacksonville, Florida, the place that we were supposed to play, it was, I believe they called it the Elks Hall, and there was a band there called Eagle Eye, he was the leader of that band. And they wouldn't let us play that place.
Eagle Eye Shields, huh?

I don't know whether he might be Eagle Eye Shields, but he was the leader of that band. Edmund Hall played with Eagle Eye Shields. Well, I'm going to get to that, Edmund Hall was at, now I ain't going to Jacksonville, but the band was consistent of, like I told you, I go back to Joy Morris on trombone, the band on trumpet, Edmund Washington on sax and clandered, Edmund Hall on sax and clandered, Albert Morgan on bass. Oh, I forgot to tell you how I went, Joy Wynn, Joy Wynn had left, had left. And that's why we hired, I forgot to see how you get tangled up, is that all right? Yeah, that's okay, don't worry. No, look, Joy Wynn left us, he got into some kind of finance trouble with Mr. Earl and Dr. Grundy, and he skipped out of town, and Chinese was round town, and we used Chinese. We used Chinese until my cousin came back. My cousin, we finally got my cousin Pete Redfield in the band, just like we had promised, we said when we get over there and find our way around, we were supposed to find Joy, we couldn't find Joy Wynn because he had his hand in with the big balls, you see. So he finally had to leave town, and we used Chinese a while, because he was around, like I said, different bands were coming in, and like I said, that was where she was living there, I said I met Sadie. Well, we had this woman, Helen Jackson, playing piano with us, and I couldn't think of the other woman we had before, the first one was there. Well anyhow, just before this trip to going to Jacksonville, Pete Redfield, my cousin got in the band. And Pete came up there, and he still had that little grudge against us, I don't know, that was his way. And we got him a place to stay, and Pete got a good friend with the landlady, and they got to be, what you say, sweethearts in their voice. And we had a lot of trouble with Pete and his drinking. Pete would get drunk and mess up and everything, and then sometimes we had to go to look for him. Well anyhow, on this trip, he was on this trip with us to Florida, I'm not sure. And like I said, when we got to Jacksonville, Florida, the place that we were supposed to play, Eagle Eye wouldn't let us work there. But we waked at Somersonic Hall, I remember, and the dance didn't go so good. And we had to wake with another band, that's my wife. They had one of those things like they had Mobile, they had a brass band playing for the people to dance by. And it was a good brass band. But when the people heard us, which they was called the Pensacola Jazz, then, that New Orleans swing and that New Orleans music we was playing, they just went wild over it. And that still kept Eagle Eye from having us playing in this place, you see. So we played a few towns out of Jackson. I remember one of the towns, I remember well, let's see now, I believe it was Olanda. I played that particular town, I remember well. And the people who had a nice crowd with me, nice, nice money on that deal. And I noticed, in all those places going out way down that way, the colored people, they get very excited. They used to drink that moonshine and thing, you know, and man, they would, it was a different kind of colored people like in New Orleans, you know, they were ready to fight and everything. And they had, they still had that eye out in the head where if you play hot, you have to play fast. But after listening to us, and the New Orleans music we're playing, they kind of caught the eye out in the way, you don't have to play fast, you know what I mean? You can still be playing hot and still be playing in a groovy tempo, you see. So getting to that same trip, so Joy and Morty, we had a meeting on the band, we're not here long. And we were what they called pro-starled and everything to vote on who wanted to go down further and who wanted to go back. Well, some of the fellas began to get a little discouraged, you know. They wanted to go back to Pensacola because we weren't making the money we thought we were going to make, you know. And the vote went against Joy of going down further in Florida, down south. I remember he mentioned Panama City and Miami and those places. And that was one of the biggest mistakes we made. Because if we had to went down there, which I found out later, because there were bands coming from that that made families like Belton, and there was another band that even went to New York, back there in the 30s. Well, those guys, and this was back in 24 and 25 I'm telling you about, you see. But at that time those guys hadn't picked up on that New Orleans piece. See, we would have made us a fortune of money.
Did you ever hear Alonzo Ross? Alonzo Ross. Alonzo Ross, he was a piano player I think over there. From where? Around Jacksonville, I think.

Well, I probably met him, a lot of the guys. He went to New York. Yeah. Well, that happened years later because now I want to get, you still get on that same kick in Jacksonville. Now, Eagle Eyes had came out somewhere and heard our band. In fact, we even went up and sat in with the band. And he liked me, who I played bands, he liked the way Alvin Morgan played the bass, and he liked the way Edmund Hall played his playing and sax. And he wanted us to quit the band. That we had always promised that we would come back to Pensacola, you see. So, I can say this, yeah, we did made our way back. We came on back to Pensacola. And our famous town was, after Pensacola, was Mobile. We always knew we could be good, but we still had that big rep, you see, around Mobile. And I remember coming back, after our first trip coming back to Pensacola, and our first trip going to Mobile, and the first trip coming back to the Mobile, Evan Hall had got a wire from this guy, Eagle Eyes. And Albert Morgan, I think, Sam Morgan was coming to Mobile kind of regularly then, and we had left Pensacola and come to Mobile this day, you see. And, well, Pope and them being a union band, we wasn't in the union, well, they made it kind of hard for us around there, you see. And we didn't do so well around there. So, first I think it was Edmund Hall left. He told me, come to me, and Albert, he said, I got this office, I'm going to save you, do y'all want to go? So, Albert was kind of discouraged. He was talking about his brother wanted to take him back home, you know, which Albert Morgan did leave there. Sam Morgan took him back to New Orleans, and I stayed around there. And, uh, uh, Edmund Hall kept on talking to me about this deal, so, it seemed that while he was in talking to me, he was looking, because he wanted, that's why he had his eyes on Cootie. So, I was on two points myself, I said, well, it looked like things ain't getting so good. Well, I really didn't want to leave the band, because the fellas had actually given me my first break, and they had a lot of hopes in me, you see. I mean, especially George Washington and Mack, you know what I mean, you see. George who? George, I mean, George Morris. That was the time I was playing. Yeah. So, like I said, we wasn't doing so well, and so, the time was coming close for Edmund Hall, he either had to take me, or he either take somebody else. So, he went and took the other guy, which was working with Homer's band, named Frank. I believe his name is Frank Jack. He took him on banjo, and he took Cootie and himself, and he, I mean, Edmund, I remember the time he had a Dodge car, and he took the, his woman, Miss Irene, and they drove to Jacksonville. And I didn't see Edmund no more, and I stayed around there a while yet, and I eventually told you all, I said, well, I think I'd best be going, I came on back home, you see. And when I came back here, I had written to my dad about a month before I was coming back, you see. Because I didn't want to put the fellas down. We had some few dates, and I went and played with them, because we used to play a lot of those out of town movies. I remember one time named Pritchett, and a couple other places, I can't think of the name. We played, but the whole of them had really got hard on us, because, apart from not being a union band and staying there, they really made it hard, because we made it, and we was taking work out of them out, you see. So like I say, I left from there, and I came back here, and we were still living up on Rampart, yeah, I believe we were still living on Rampart 360, 20, 20, I think we were still living up there, yeah. Well, anyhow, my daddy had an all-in-range with me to work with B.B. Risley had broke up the Tuxedo band, him and Celestane had fell out, and he had a group, and Celestane had a group. And B.B. Risley had the job on the Pelican, and his brother was running the Pelican for fallback, and it was a beautiful place. And so I went down in a rehearsal with him one night, and I had a fellow named Willie Bonte, I'd be playing banjo with him. And at that same time, they had originally had asked me about Alfred Morgan, and Alfred Morgan was already in time, I think he was playing with Rene, he had got him a job. Because I mean, like I said, a good musician, when you're a good musician, you get around, people know you, and you can play, and you know, you'll always get your job. So he had wanted to change bass on, you know, did I ever wake up there? Yeah, he did wake up there a while. He always wanted to change, you know, so I said, yeah, I was a good musician. I said, I've just been playing with Rene, and so Al would wait for us a while. And then David Jones came. David Jones had been here, I believe, I hadn't known him. So he got David Jones. But David Jones had told himself that he had went up, when he came here, he went up to the guy to try to get in the roof garden. Well, he couldn't get in that band, because they had been together so long. Willie Humphrey had been in there with Manuel Perez, and Capri, and that same group, they had been again a long time, you see. And then he, some kind of way, he picked up on B'Bare, really. So he got in the band. Well, the band already had, they had Robert Hall, and they had another fellow named Joe Watson, that was a very good saxophone and clarinet player. That was two, yeah. And Schatz was already in that band. They had another trumpet player named, and he was a little black and white fellow. He used to be a prize fighter. I don't know what that fellow's name. He's out in El Paso now. Bat Brown, had him on trumpet. And Emma Bauer on piano. And I believe he had Happy, yeah, Happy Playing Drum. Happy Playing Drum. So we, that band, built up to be a pretty good band on the Pelican, because we would rehearse and we would get good arrangement down through the direction of David John. David John had charge of what they called being the director and leader of the band. And we would take, buy the stock numbers and take them and change them around. And David John had a good idea of, he could write music and he could give a man a note. He could take his sax section and say, you take this note and this note, he'd take the brass section and say, you all take this note and this note. And he had already had experience playing with Fred Marl for years back, which you remember reading in history. So we built up a great band up there. They used to call us the Great Pelican Band. And they used to have, in them days they used to have what they called, the nights they'd have two bands. In other words, there was a book between the roof guard and the pelican in those days. And I had went back to, I had brought my violin back to Pensacola. I forgot to tell you about that. But I eventually got away from violin, so they knew how I played violin. So I used to bring my violin, a couple of them I used to play on the walls, you know, but I had kind of just got, because I found there wasn't no money. Most things wasn't no money to me, but playing the violin, you see. And so I think why I say I stuck most to playing the banjo. Now, as I said, oh yeah.
Oh, excuse me. Did you say who the piano player was originally? Emma Barron.

Emma Barron. Yeah, Emma Barron. I'll call them again if you want. No, no. Emma Barron was the piano. She was already with the bass, see. But now Celestan, when he had his band, his band was, Celestan on trumpet, I believe he had Bill Matthews on trombone, and he had, who was his, his clarinet, yeah, his sax player was this boy Walter, Polo, or what is it? Polo Barnes.
Polo Barnes.

He had, they had him so long on that number, Josephine. They were still popping on that number, and he had played that famous saxophone solo on that, see. And in his rhythm section, who was on drums? I know John Moray was still on banjo, and I think Simon was living here, I think Simon was playing bass with him. And who do you have on drums?
Was this after Chani or before?
No, this is way after Chani time, Chani, that's been the year after that.
Was it when Zaire was with him or after?
I can't think of who his drummer was at that time. Must have been one of those good ones.
Snaggs maybe? No, you know.
Did you know Snaggs?
Yeah, yeah. Where was he from while we were on the Sunday?

I don't exactly know, I believe Snaggs was one of those guys who used to go around with shows a lot of business, you know, you'd see him in town, he'd come in town, because he was a very eccentric drummer.
Mm-hmm.
Yeah. But I don't know.
By eccentric drummer you mean?

I mean he was a guy who was playing shows, I mean you, besides playing regular dance drum, you could do a lot of showing off and clowning, you know. And still he was a good dance drummer, you see. Yeah, that's what I mean by that. And then he had a lot of things I think, you know, little diddies you used to see, always make people look at him, you see. He could, you know, he was a guy who could always get him a job at any band, you know, to be glad to have him, you see. Yeah, so we're still about the Pelican, now that band went.
Excuse me for interrupting, I wanted to ask what kind of a place it was. I was in there once and ate dinner, but where was the dance hall? Upstairs.
Upstairs. It was only a two-story building. In that time, you mean in the 50s or the 40s?
In the 40s, in 1942, right?

Well at that time it was, they either had a till or something, then they had some kind of GI schooling up there. They had a barber school up there I believe, when I came back in in 49. I don't think there was much dancing up there, anything.
But the whole second floor was one big dance hall?

One just like a, yeah, it run the whole width of the place. Well like I say, going back to there, now they had other places running in that vicinity, the Astoria was running. Then they had another place on Grabber Street, between Ramport and Drys, upstairs, was running. In other words, you had four places running in that vicinity. You had the Roof Court and the Pelican, the Astoria, and this place on Grabber Street. And that's what I remember, when I came back at that time, I think there was a guy, I think Chris Keller was waking up there, and maybe, maybe Punch if he was here. And another fellow I believe, what do you call this, this fellow? I think, I remember Chris Keller, well there was one of them kind of low down blues places, this place on Grabber Street, between Ramport and Drys. And then, yeah, I think Rene was playing, I think it was Rene playing at Astoria, for Beansy, up there. And the Roof Court had a Manupurrius band, well, yeah, you remember, set up there. Well, there was a big competition between the Roof Garden and the Pelican. When the Pelican, the Pelican announced, we're gonna have two bands, so those two bands would be mostly like on a Monday or Wednesday night. See, those halls would run like Monday, Wednesday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday would run, and I believe Wednesday, I don't think it was Monday. Now, sometime on the Monday they would have to bring the people out there, they'd have a two band dance. And I remember this world, if Roof Gordon would advertise a two band, Richard, Manuel Ridgely would say, well, we're gonna have three, excuse me, we're gonna have three bands. And then they went high, I remember one time having four bands.
All the bands.

Yeah, and those bands were like, I remember well, and then the band off the boat, Faith Marble off the boat, they used to hire him sometimes to play because they would come after their job. You see, their job would close about twelve o'clock, and they would come and play, the dance would last, well, maybe about three o'clock, something, two-thirty or three o'clock. See, well that was an added attraction, see, where people would come out there because they couldn't hear the Faith Marble band on the boat, you know, because that was the white boat, see. Well that would draw people, and then there was another thing, they used to have a band from, they had this band from Natchez. What's that guy named? He had a name around Natchez, like Cleveland Williams had a name around Donisonville. What was that name?
Did you ever hear Bud Scott or Walter Vons up there? In Natchez, by the way, where we were mentioning? Bud Scott?
Yeah, that's the name I'm thinking about, Bud Scott. He was a national name around Natchez, like Cleveland Williams was around Donisonville.
What did Bud Scott do? I want to get this started.

Well I believe if he didn't play it he was a great singer. And he was one of those guys that could make up his own song, rhyme a song, and he had a good powerful voice. The band couldn't play any louder and he could sing. And the band was built around him, from what I understand. Was he a big guy, a little guy? I think he was a kind of big fellow. Big head, I think. I think he had, to me, he had a pitch of something like that. He had a pitch of something like Jan Brushing that used to play with Count Basin, one of those kind of voices too. Well anyhow, we used to have Excursion used to come here. And when Excursion would come from Natchez, they drew a lot of people, colored people. Well, I mean, the Manu Ridge would hire that band to come down, you see. And then from Donisonville, I remember, and that would be a contest there. That was all to draw the people and draw the crowd, see. And the Pelican band, if we didn't win some time, they'd have it fixed so that they would just give it to the band. They would just give it to the band to make the people come out to Natchez, see. Then they'd have a band from Donisonville came down one time, Clayborne Williams. Well, Manu originally, he'd tell me that he used to play, well his brother said he used to play a peck home, but he never was a great musician, but he loved music, you see. And he was running the place for Paul Packer and he just did whatever he wanted. And that was his pleasure, listening to those bands from Natchez and the band from, Clayborne Williams band from Donisonville. Now, on this particular night we had this buck with Clayborne Williams band, it was really a kick. They drew a lot of people, because they had a lot of people here from Donisonville, you know, and the place was packed and they made money off it, you know. So, I think it was a cup. I know they were one of those, you know, trophy cups, you know. And they had a place running. Beansy was running the place, a couple of doors from the Pelican. I can't think of the name of them, but it was a gambling and the Apple's Union still in prohibition, you know. You could go there and get you whatever you want, you know. And we used to go there and sell it. After we'd get to the dance, we'd want to drink, we'd go there and Manu was selling the stuff too in this place, Paul Packer. But we'd go there and drink. For this particular night we had this contest with Clayborne Williams band. All of us, our band, well those that wanted to drink and those with Clayborne Williams band, got together and we drank there until about five o'clock in the morning, drinking out the trophy cup. See, well, it's my time to fill it up. And Manu, we got some drug. And like I said, well the Pelican band went on. Oh, who won the contest? Well, it was one of those kind of mutual deals, I think, and they might have had two cuppers. I know who he had. Imagine he didn't want to make Clayborne no set, because Clayborne actually drew the people, you see. Now he had a nice band, but I mean our band was just a little advanced, you know what I mean. Because right there in the city, the stuff that David John was putting down was a little modern than what Clayborne had. Now he had a good band, I believe that. Because he drew as many people as we did. He'd come out to hear the band from that, been here and lived with my father and mother. All of them was out, you know, to come out because that's my mother's home, you see.
Could Clayborne Williams' band fake it all then?

Well they could, but he stuck most of the music. They always did, stuck most of the music. Like I said, the band on the Pelican, we had music, but we had head numbers we did and everything, yeah. Now, and we'll get back to the same thing on the Pelican. And those three and four piece bands they used to have up there. I remember there was a band that used to come up there, there was a guy named One Eye Babe who played bass and that was Gashun's father. And they had what they used to call them, when the band could swing and had a good detail, they called them a gut bucket band. That was a real low down gut bucket music, you know, and these guys could really do that. And they used to come up there with Sam Red Allen, he's come and play with that band. They had this man, One Eye Babe, on bass. I can't think who the drummer had his son, Gashun, on banjo. I don't know who the trombone player was.
Now Gashun, is that Joe Phillips?
No, no, Gashun is, well that's all I would do, but I knew his father was a bass player. They called him One Eye Babe, and that old man could pull some- Gashun drives for-
He drives for Pete Herman. That's the same guy, sir.

I can tell you, I remember when he first came in, that Sam man was just like those boys playing blues on a guitar, playing with their fingers like them rock and roll, that man was doing it back in them days.
He can do it still, huh?

Well I haven't heard of playing guitar in many years. And then just like the other guys, he went from guitar to the band, you see, like everybody did, the guitar got kind of dazed and the band would come out when he went to that. He was a good band player. He was a good band player.
While we're on the subject of fingerstyle, where did you first pick up on that? Where did you first see that?

Well that's where my daddy played guitar. He never used a pick. He never used a pick? No, my daddy played with his fingers. And he had a rhythmic stroke and in fact he couldn't play with a pick. He tried, he just couldn't play. That's the way he learned how to play.
He didn't use any finger picks or anything?
He didn't use no thumb. No thumb at all? Some guys used a thumb pick. My daddy didn't use that. And he could play a nice chord, he could play a melody with chords.
And would he play a six string guitar for? That's what he played.
My daddy liked a six string guitar. And he wouldn't use his thumb?
No. I noticed most of those guys use a thumb to play the bass part.
Yeah, but he had that callous, I mean he could get just as loud a tune as you want like that. I'll be.
That's right.
Now- Can you play fingerstyle?
Well I could do nothing but not too much.
It's a thing you got to practice in food and do it. I wouldn't say I was good, I could do it.
Is there anybody today who can really play blues that way?
Oh yeah.
In town. In town, who would you say?

Well I'll tell you, this particular young guy over there, I say he's younger than me, a guitar slim. That's the way he plays. He plays with his fingers. And there's a couple of others, I can't think of that amp at the moment now, but they play with their fingers. Of course they have that electric guitar and they have that amp way up you know.
And that runs everything.

Well I mean that rock and roll, that's the way he's doing it. And I mean with this particular guy I say guitar slim, I know there's a couple of others down there. I mean of course he's right for me, I think when I mention him. Yeah.
What about banjo, how did they tune them in the old days? Everybody used a four string tenor or a spectrum or five string?

Well I can tell you about that. When the banjo, now when they had banjos in the band like I said, they were using the guitar banjo. Because Johnny, not only Johnny's sincere, there was a couple of other guys around there. A fellow named Lorenzo Starr. They used a banjo guitar. In fact like I said before I started playing professional in 24, before the banjo got popular, that's what they were using. And that thing had a pretty good carrying power. Because I remember there was a guy with Sam Morgan band, that was before Johnny something played with him. Johnny Dave. Johnny Dave, before Johnny Dave. And those guys didn't carry no piano. No sir, they didn't carry no piano. And that thing had a man good carry and those guys really played good chords. You know, as far as their ear training would tell them, see. Yeah. And then like I say, when some of the guys, when them, I don't know why they were just a style I imagine, when they went to the tenor banjo, they tuned, some of them tuned the tenor banjo like the four strings only on the guitar. They played the same chord, but the only thing they didn't have that A and the E string, you see. Then eventually some of them, they just went on after that, they said, well now I want to learn the real tenor banjo. They went to the tenor banjo play. See. Yeah. So this band on the Pelicans stayed together. Well like I said, we created a lot of fame, which we didn't make no record, which was hard to do back in those days. And Maniel, I mean, maybe Ridgely, some kind of way he had a little fall and I with his brother Maniel and we left there and we went to, there was a fellow named, all I know him by name is Jack Sheen, they call him the Coconut King. He opened up a place, he built a place called Suburban Garden. And we went out there, I think that's in the St. Bernard Parish because it's right near the river. Way up there?
Yeah, whittown there.
Jefferson.
Jefferson, yeah.

Jefferson, yeah. Jefferson, yeah. And this new place, we actually opened that place up. We had gambling and everything. Well, they had one of those things where the sheriff got mad and everything, they'd come in and rage, you know, if he wasn't paying off and see, well, it happened that it got a little hot out there and it got the radio too much and this guy, Jack Sheen, just decided to close down, you see.
Not to interrupt, but what did Ridgely play at that time? What instruments?
Tramble!
Only.
Well, at that time, yeah, yeah. Of course, I was told he played bass, he played a little bass, then he went to, well, after playing drum, now that came about later.
Yeah, well, I wanted to straighten that out. Yeah, yeah. The Beverly, the place is now called the Beverly Garden, or it was a few years ago. Maybe it is, but it is, yeah, yeah.
Maybe it is the same place. I know that place was likely built new when we went out there and we made it.
Towards the river from the Jefferson Highway?
Yes, it was not far from the levee.
Because you go out the highway, it was closer to the river.

Yeah, closer to the river, that's right. Yeah, I believe it was the Beverly Garden. Well, anyhow, when, after they let us off, well, that particular time, I used to do this, you'd get a place to call the entertainment club. Well, all the musicians used to hang around there and we used to go down there and, like if we had a job, we'd go sit in with the band and, you know, jam session. And, um, Faith Marvel band, all the band used to hang around there when they'd get off in their wake, you know, and, well, I had to change musicians to go around there to make yourself known and be seen, you see. And, um, Faith was, um, had an idea, he was, he was going to change banjo and he was using, uh, the Willie Forrestone banjo. And, uh, he had heard me in and I had a brother, my brother was working out on the boat, uh, not as a musician, but as a deckhand or pole or something like that. And he had been telling him about me, you know. So, uh, Faith one morning come down there and I made it, just pay attention to me and I heard me playing everything. And, well, that time, numbers like that, if you could play like the world waiting for the sunrise, if you could play Tiger Rag on the banjo or any number that you could feature on the banjo those days, you know, you would consider. And I always, like a guy, always kept up what was going on, you see. So, um, he heard me and he said, well, I want you to come out to rehearsal. He said, if you can mess. I heard about your reading and everything. He said, I, uh, I would like to get you, uh, there was a fellow on the trumpet player named Albert Snyder. He was on the boat and he spoke for me, see. Well, they knew about my reading, see. So, I, I went out to the rehearsal and, and I must have did good because, uh, next thing I think the next week or so they had me in the banjo, see. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Okay, we're back to Willie Foster now.

Yeah, so I said I've taken Willie Foster's job on the boat, and in that band was Freight Marble as leader, and the rhythm section had a fellow named Slim on drum, they had Alvin Morgan on bass, and me on banjo, and the reed section was Willie Humper was in the reed section, had another fellow named Rylan, that's two, and another fellow named Mason, I believe it was Mason, he's a famous trumpet player out of St. Louis.
Norman Mason?

Norman Mason played trumpet and sax. Sax, yeah, he's a very good eccentric man, and in the brass section had Albert Snire, and they had a fellow, Albert Snire on trumpet, and another fellow, he's in Chicago now, he was a very good reader, but he never could take a hot chorus, and the trombone player was Nat Story, that was the brass section.
And another, the trumpet you say was a, never could take a hot chorus?

Well, Eckerhardt, Lewis Eckerhardt, that's what it was, yeah. He seemingly was a fellow just out of, youngster just out of school and everything, but he was a very good musician, he could read anything, but his lips didn't allow him to go too high, and they kept him on second, you see, and they tried a couple of times to put him on lead, but he just didn't have the punch to play a solo, or even take a hot solo, you see. At that particular time, but he eventually learned later on. So as I say, I worked on a boat that particular year, I played that season here, and I went to St. Louis, and I played the fourth season, but during that season in St. Louis, they were still dicking on time to get a fellow, but they had before me, before Willie Foster, what was his name? He was a little short, but he looked like a white man to me. He used to be with the Cab Calloway band when he was on Chicago, his name would come to me. He was a very eccentric banjo player. He was a novelty man, he could sing, he could entertain, because I remember there was one song out that had what they call a parody to it, he was very good on, Laugh Clown Laugh, I remember that well. Well at that time I didn't do nothing but play, I didn't sing, I even couldn't talk a song or nothing, so there was a Captain John on the boat, he used to always tell me, he said, why don't you try to do some little thing besides just playing, you see. He said, you know Red was a, that was his name was Red, that's what it was. He said Red was a, well he was a clown in the world, he could do everything, you see, put the banjo around his neck and everything, you see, and that's what people like, you see, and even sing. So Captain Joe used to come down and rehearse a band sometimes in St. Louis, and he, I remember one time he started me to sing a number, I mean his name of the song was about, sing something about Hallelujah in it, and another song he had me used to get up there, he even showed me how to do it, well, that went over pretty good, you see. Well all this, the whole time St. Louis they was trying to get Red, but they couldn't get him, you see, so that's where I met my, the first woman I married, my first wife named Alma, you see, and I eventually played the season in St. Louis, so on the way coming back to New Orleans, I got the word that Red was going to meet the boat in Memphis, and that's where I would be discharged, you see. So at that time they always had the word on the boat when you're going to know it's going to get fired, they used to have the sail, well the axe is going to drop on sail, they call it the axe. The axe was the boat, you know, the carriage that actually used for the, you know, like that person having a fire, you know, and those things, and they say, well man, the axe is on you now. And Faith used to have a piano song about don't talk about me when I'm gone, and everybody said, well, no, somebody leaving. Well, the only thing I didn't take it so hard, because I had the opportunity to see many guys go when I was there, you know. So they were very good to me, the Stratford Company, they had let me go a week before my time, I mean a couple days before my time, and they paid me for that week, and they gave me, they always give you a bonus, you know, like when you make that particular season, I got that back, and I stayed on Memphis about a week or so.
Well, to interrupt you again, would the Stratford Spiders musicians or anything? Oh yes, yes.

Now they were, like Captain Brown that I know played the violin, and some of them, like Captain Joe, I learned to play the piano. And they really knew me. They knew how, I tell you what I would know is they were good at, you see, making your program on that boat. Your music had to be timed to get a certain many numbers within the program. The program ran from about four, and they always had what they call side numbers, you see, and you always had to have numbers, you had to time yourself, a certain program, and the program ran from about one to fourteen. Then you had two parts of that program, or three parts of it where you played a waltz set, you see. And that music had to be timed so that you had to get so many numbers within a program. And they had that time of timing music by watching a watch. They could tell you just what tempo, because fate, that was one thing a leader had to be very precise in the knocking off a tempo if it was supposed to be forty or fifty or sixty, like that, metronome beats, you know. You had to be very careful about that. And they had numbers that they didn't want you to play too fast and not too slow. And down in Yaw Range there was a certain way you had to play when you got to St. Louis. There was a different way. In St. Louis you had to play a more fast tune, because they were dancing that Lindy Hoppin thing back in that time. And that's why I actually hadn't had the experience of playing the fastest tempo I ever played playing music, especially when we got to St. Louis. So getting on back to you, so when I came back here ...
Oh, we left out in Memphis in town.

Yeah, as I said, I was fired in Memphis, you see. So I stayed around Memphis and had a little fun around Beale Street and things. I was staying in a hotel there, and I was married to my wife and we were coding there, and she came up there because she was from Jackson, Tennessee, but she lived in St. Louis then. And so she went back to her home and I came back down here. Well I was like a guy who had to start looking around and everything, you know.
Was there much music on Beale Street? Was it like New Orleans?

Well Beale Street I tell you was an exciting street to see on a Saturday. It was just a particular Saturday to me at that time. And I used to just like to walk up and down and just look at the sights and go in and different dumbs and dive and different things and everything. It was really something to see. Did you have piano players? Well most places had like little piano players. There was one place where there might have been a union or it might have been a congregation where the musicians used to meet. I used to go around there and I was calling the fellas name. I don't remember the name.
Was it near Pee Wee's place?
It was on Beale Street I remember.
Near Pee Wee's place?

Around in that neighborhood? The only thing I remember, I remember there was a colored theater and there was one place we used to go, like I used to go eat. And you could drink like, you know, during probation days and get whiskey and things. But, yeah, when this fella Red came on the boat and work, well like I said, I was still around Memphis because I had gotten my hotel room and he and I feel like we were still on a good time. It wasn't long. So we went up with them one night for this particular place. I believe it was named the Panama or the paddock or something place. I went up there was a hotel and a saloon or something down at the bottom or a barbershop, see, colored fellas running. We stayed up there that morning and I was with them. I said, I grew friendly around the mountain, Alma, and we had a terrific time up there. We drank and I got to be good friends with this fella Red, you see. So like I said, I left, she went back to Tennessee and Jack Tennessee and I came on back home. Well, coming back here, like I said, I had to start looking around, you know. So I think coming back, I think I went back with the Bay Rizzle band. And that was the time that he had put the trombone down and was playing drum. And we used to rehearsal back at Emma House, I remember, on Short Street. And that's the time I met Gilbert, we were just coming up, Gilbert Young was coming up playing. They had him on trumpet, Emma Bauer on piano, me on banjo. And I believe Happy was playing drum with him, I think then, again. And I believe Joe Watson was still living. And I don't think David Jones was with him, I don't think so, maybe he was. But anyhow, I didn't work with him too long. And who did I get with then? I think I got with... No, no. I had before then doing him, I was working at Jitney dancers, yeah. Because John Maria was working at a place called, one of those Jitney places, on Iberville. What's the name of that place? Near the fern? The fern wasn't, it wasn't the fern, it was the fern and something else.
Budweiser? Was it near the Budweiser?

Well, maybe this was the fern, it was the Budweiser and the fern, they were right next to each other. The Vila was the La Vila? La Vila, that's it, that's it. Yeah. John Maria had charge of that job, and he had... It was his job, John Maria to banjo. Well, like I said, I used to always go around, you see. In fact, I can tell you, there's a different place, they had a different place on St. Charles and Cronolette. They had one on Burgundy and Canal. And then, like you said, the La Vila and the Vila were right next to each other, you see. Well, and often, you go around those places and you'd say, well, I ain't doing, I'm not doing anything. You go around and the guys will let you play a while, you see. And then, you know, sometimes a guy takes sick and he says, well, I want you to sail tonight. So I used to go around with La Vila and John, and then those guys were particularly who they'd let play, because if you wasn't a good player, they wouldn't let you play, you see. So I'd go around there and arrest John up a while, and John would go and steal Howard. So, well, the guys wouldn't worry because they knew I could hold a job down. Well, in that band was Joe Robichaud on piano, Thero Poitain on alto, and Albert Martin, we call them Fats on drums. Is that right? Yeah, they didn't use no bass in those bands. No, they didn't use no bass, no. Look at that. I see it. Lee Collins on trumpet, Thero on alto sax, and Joe Rocha on piano, and Fats on drum, and John Murray on banjo. Yeah. So John was going to New York, you see. And there was another fella named Willie Conray. Willie Conray. Well, like John, like I said, he was the idle banjo player at that time. And everybody used to like to copy. I myself used to copy behind him, you see. And there was another Willie Conray. Willie Conray, I found I was supposed to get that job too. But anyhow, the job finally came to me. And at that same time, they had hired David Jones. They put David, they had, in other words, the guy had so much fluent with the proprietor. In other words, if he liked the guy, well, the guy's technically liked David Jones. David Jones wasn't doing nothing. So they hired him on the job. So that made two sax, and a trumpet, and three rhythm, you see. So we stayed there, and Lee Collins, and David Jones got to dickin' with Beansley, who run Astoria now. Beansley wanted to have a club, want to have a nightclub on Astoria, and they had a show here, that was stranded, a full good show. I think the lyrics must have been running them days. And he had an idea of, and Cook's, Sherman Cook was the famous MC in those days. And he had an idea of building up a, and that was a big place that we would have been up there, that story upstairs. Of having a band like Lee Collins, because Lee Collins had been playing for those guys, like in the town, different places way back in those days, you see. And so when we got the job, and we built up a terrific band there. With those, let's say, and that band, I believe, Albert Morgan, that's how we put Albert Morgan on bass, yeah. And Albert Morgan on bass, that's what Astoria Strutt come about. Had Albert Morgan on bass, me on banjo, and John Robichaud on piano, had David Jones and Theta on sax, and Lee Collins on trumpet. And man, you talking about a gut bucket band, boy, we used to gut. And then David Jones, like I say, we didn't hear no music, but he could tell a guy, I said, well man, you use this note, you take this note. And we'd have a little introduction, and we'd have, like if Lee Collins was taking a solo, he'd have this, him and Theta would be blowing a jazz background, you see, they'd make it all up here, you know. And all of us loved to drink, man, we had a ball of tea. So, here come a fella named Don Albert, out of Texas. Don Albert, he come in y'all with some money, and he come in y'all to build him up a band. So, I think Albert had left, Albert Morgan had left, and went on the boat, back on the boat again, yeah. So, before that, before I got to get a story, we had made a record, that's how this Astor Strutton thing come about. Yeah, we had a record too. Yeah, so Lee Collins had met, I think it was the Sam Guy and Mirs, or something like that.
Well, they didn't, yeah, that's Astor Strutton.

So, Lee Collins got into thinking about the record man in town. So, he said, man, I got a record date. He said, man, I want some original tune. He said, man, the man that come up and heard, he said, we didn't know he was here, but he was back there. And I said, at that time, white people used to come to the Astor and they had a terrific flow show up there. So, Sherman Cook was the master of show em on it, they had two fellas who used to dance, they were good. And they had a little short dog woman who had a very pretty voice, sing a song. And they had another woman from St. Louis, it was Joe Robichaud lady. And they had a, yeah, and we had a good flow show, you know what I mean? And we used to pack that place. And they used to, white people used to come in there. I remember guys like Frederica Ford and Beans and his white people used to come up there. Well, they sat in their place, you know what I mean? They didn't make them, but they used to come, like to be around, come listen to the colored music and look at the colored shows, you know? So, like I said, another thing, we used to have to advertise there. We used to have to go on the truck and have to go around the city and advertise. And then when we get through the truck, they had a little, used to have a little, uh, balcony, balcony. Coming from the dance hall and we'd get out there and play about 15 or 20 minutes. Right on Rampart Street. Right on Rampart Street. And man, that street would be like a, it wouldn't be no holiday. Would it be like a holiday because I know the Paris prison wasn't so far from there. And the police used to have to come down there because they was blocking the truck.
Did anybody play clarinet with you regularly? No, that fella playing the clarinet.

Well, I will tell you now, after I got to tell you about that story, after we rehearsing those numbers down, and David Jones, we took certain numbers. I can't tell, I can tell you the name. And made, and used our own ideas that were based on certain numbers, like Sensation and Ray. That was called, our own, it was called another name. And we took Sister Kate. And just used the chords, but I was on and voiced it down. Didn't use the melody. You see, everybody was doing that in those days. You see? And, um, that particular, let me see what that is. Anyhow, when we got to the, when we got to, didn't have no, the attire. That's me there on the band. I was a pretty good picker back in those days. And there was another guy that graded me, named Kathy Dow. Kathy could do some picking.
Yeah.

Yeah. So, when we got, we made the record, I was down there at the old Italian Hall on Espinay. And they had, what they call a master disc, about this big. The electric, I think, had just about come out then, you know. And the hardest thing we had was getting the drums, not to be too loud, and the album morgan on the bass. And when we got down there, that's when I met Sidney Arden. I had been seeing him around, and I heard him play, and that guy's a terrific player. He could play just like, there was very few white boys in those days who could play like colored. But Sidney Arden could sound, I mean to me he sounded just as good as Bayshade, or Edmund Hall, which I had worked with in those days. And I was amazed how white men could play a clarinet that good. That's right. So, we, I know we'd have, and Albert Morgan used to, the man would have Albert Morgan in the place, and when they would get rid of the record, Albert Morgan would sneak up because he wanted to be hood. And he could play that bass, something loud, man. So the most trouble we got, because we had the numbers all time and everything, you see, was getting the drum, the drum had to use pillars, man. And then the guy used to stomp his foot, you know. So the man had to lean, mostly everybody, man, he had to use pillars. A pillar where everybody said he wouldn't take that, you know. But anyhow, the record, the record's, uh, now Sidney, I don't remember Sidney Arden had nothing in the hustle, was it? He just came on down there, and we told him, I said, I want you to take a, you come in on this part. And he'd fill in there. And the blues, the Damp Weather Blues, how that came, that title came about, it was raining like a sun on that day, and we had our little shot with us, you know, whiskey or moonshine, whether it was in the day. And it was kind of cool in that place, and we were drinking that to keep warm, to give us the spirit. And they said, the man, when they come down the city, he wanted some blues, let's make up some blues. So we decided to call that Damp Weather. And there's a particular part of that blues where I was supposed to take a solo, and Joe Rose started off so much, so I just let him go through, see. But the other numbers, we had already hoist them, you know what I mean, we had them down time and everything.
You had the tippies, where did that come from?

I think that was, that was taken from Sidney, like I said, it was kind of high, and they used to call it, used to avoid, you're kind of tipsy when you're drunk, you know. It was, all those things come up about slang, you know. Yeah. Slang, yeah. And the other number, we just named like we was waking on Astor, we called that Astor, a strut. And what was the other one named? Duet Stump. Duet Stump, well Duet Stump is based, the chord changes, based on Sister Kate, but it's played in the fans' tempo. And David Jones and Lee Collin used to play so much trumpet on that number, not only that, so David Jones and Thuttle got together and got that saxophone chromatic going up and down like that. That's how they got, that's strictly from here. David Jones would make the first part and he'd say, well Thuttle you take this. And after he'd give it to Thuttle and get it, then he'd put a second to it. And I mean that thing, just like at the record, we used to have them people jumping on those two numbers. They didn't, before we recorded, they didn't know what it was until when we made the recording, the radio station, they'd give us a nice plug-in. I mean we made a nice famous name for ourselves at that time, see, but all we got paid was for the recording. But one thing I did know, it did put me in a book, because Lee had got a book when I saw him in Chicago, wrote by a Frenchman. And they had my name in there, you see. Now, after that we stayed up there a while.
One more question on the record. Who did the singing?

Oh yeah, the singing came about, and that came about, Alvin Morgan always could, you like to sing and scat like, looks like everybody was trying to do that, see. And Alvin could do that, so he was the one decided to say, yeah, well let me scat this, and say, let me take one on scat, you see. And I think that was supposed to be a band or solo for them, so as he did it so good, they just let it go through at that, you see. That was Alvin Morgan during the scatting, yeah. Al Morgan? Yeah, Al Morgan, yeah. His name was Alvin Morgan. That's where he looks today. Yeah, oh the hell yeah. The last time I saw him in Chicago, I was with Johnny and Lindsey, a bass player, he was with my group I had up there. And he was with some band, and they had a little layover there. And it was during the holidays, I remember, we had him over to Johnny and Lindsey's house, and I had a band. I had a group up there, it was two guitars, myself on guitar, and Kazma on guitar, Johnny and Lindsey on bass, and had a fellow named Artere on piano. And they went around to Johnny and Lindsey's house, and he had good old red beans and gumbo and everything, and we had a ball. Yeah, old Al Morgan. That looks good. Well anyhow, so, like I said, Don Albert came in town to build up a band, and that's, and he took, he broke up, he took men out of Sydney band, I think he took men out of Celestan band, and he took our drummer, Fat, because Al Morgan had left and went back with Feed Marlboro, yeah. And, uh.
Took men out of Sydney's band? Who's Sydney? Sydney Desby.

I see. Yeah, I believe he took one of the, Herbert Hall out of that band, a saxophone player. And, uh, he had a band, well, he can, he can hear you going all around. Well, he came to me, and, uh, told me about the deal. Well, I was kind of a little sick then, and my wife then was working as a waitress at the Pelican, and I was working up there on that story. And, uh, I had an offer to Sydney Desby to go on the boat, see. The season on the boat opens up around, I think around about April and May. So, I thought about it, I say, uh, I had worked on the boat with Fate, and I say, I know that's pretty good money. I mean, you know, in other words, it's a job you know you're going to get paid, you don't have to worry, and you stay there, you live, your expense don't cost you nothing, you get your straight salary, you know. And I said, well, this will give me a little chance to kind of get out of the hole, you know. And, uh, so, I tried everything. He was, he wanted to give me, like, he was giving fellas $20, and some guys he gave $50, you know, to go away with him. But, I didn't, I didn't take that deal with him. And, uh, well, I don't go away from the man that was down. Well, anyhow, I went on the boat. Well, when I went on the boat, uh, Danny Barker was working up on, uh, on a place on, on, on, on, on the canal in Burgundy, with, uh, with Willie Pajo and a woman, you see, I believe Sonny, Sonny was on the trombone, I believe Saeed was on the drum up there, and another fella got killed, John something clown that, he plays clown that, he got killed, yeah, in California. And, uh.
Had a woman piano player?
Yeah, had a woman piano player. I'm trying to think of her name. I know that woman well. She lived there on any street near Claiborne.
Is that Edna? No, not Edna.

No, not Edna. Willamina something. Willamina Borg. Yeah, Willamina Borg, yeah, yeah. So, uh, Danny was working up there and he hadn't so long, hadn't too long got married. And, uh, like he got married working on that job, yeah. So, he was good friends with Lee and also I was good friends with Danny, you know. So, they had a trip, this fella Sherman Cooks had a trip to, had an excursion trip to go to Chicago, you see. And, uh, Lewis Armstrong at the time was living in Chicago, you see. And, uh, Lee was telling me, man, this is my good time to get to meet my good buddy Lewis and get a chance to be around Chicago. Because, Lee had been up there before, you see. And I had, well, that was three offers I had at the same time, you know. So, I thought, I said, well, no, the best thing for me to do is go and take this job on the board. I said, I know it. If I make that season, I said, that's gonna be, you know, have a nice, but I'll get myself straightened out and do things for my wife and things. And, uh, Don Apple, I had to turn him down. So, I recommended that Danny would, would be the one to take, take the job if he wanted to, see. So, and also, um, Paul Barber was in, in Chicago with Lewis Armstrong and that, that's, uh, kind of Danny's uncle, I believe, something like that. Mm-hmm. Yeah. So, Danny wanted to see him. You see, in other words, Danny was trying to get away from here, the branch his way so he could get somewhere, you see. So, that was, uh, those were the three mistakes I made. I should have stayed there. So, those guys, they, they went to Chicago. In other words, the band went and the band got paid and the band, you know, they played a few numbers on the train. And they tell me when they got to Chicago, they even did like they did in the Orleans. They went on the truck and advertised, you know, around. And they went with Lewis and Lewis went, went with them and see, they had a ball, man. So, that's where Danny met his uncle, uh, Paul. And Paul, they must have got again and told him, say, well, you can, I can see that you, you'll get, uh, you'll get something, see if you just come on up here. And they must have been, Paul, and that time Lewis must have been figuring on going to New York, see. So, anyhow, Lewis and Paul, Paul was working with Lewis Armstrong, they didn't go to New York. And I don't know whether Danny went to Chicago or went to Winston Hill, but anyhow, it was through Paul, I think, that got him open. And then Danny went to Chicago, then maybe went to New York. Well, I didn't see Danny for a long time, boy, and I heard he'd been playing with bands like the Blue, Blue something band around New York. In other words, he had made contact with the big fellas, you see. The next thing I heard he was, excuse me, was with the, with Cab Calloway band, you see. So, like I said, I mean, that could have been a break for me, but I did make the seat with Sidney. I came back here and I stayed with Sidney band. I remember I was living on, on Prairie and La Hoppe. I was still with my first wife and Randy Hall, which became the, it was another band, young band, a fellow younger me was becoming to be a good banjo player and arranger. I was doing arranging myself in those days. I was staying with Gene Ware and his wife, Zareta, and my, me and my wife, Alma, we were staying on Prairie and La Hoppe. And Randy Hall was staying right across the street from us and they had another fellow named Reuben Hughes. In other words, it was a kind of little musician's center all staying around up in that thing, you know what I'm saying? And we all were working with Sidney. So, this thing got a little rough with Sidney and Gene had, had went and got him a job at one of the Jitney places, see. It might have been the foreign, you see. Well, then the WPA band was out, you could go join them, but I always, I was a guy like this. I said, well, I could always get out here and, and what you call, pick up or hustle a little more work, because I was working with Black Sidney band. And I'd come out here and work around Decatur Street, around French Street up in there, and when the band wasn't doing nothing, it would be like, I mean I was playing still playing banjo, like banjo and piano, and piano and piano and drumming the horn, and work maybe two or three nights a week, see. Then when the band would get something like this time here, the band would be plenty busy, you see. But like after Mardi Gras, things would drop, you see. And that's the time when we'd go around and get these little jobs. And then somehow I used to work out.
You never did join the WPA band then?

No, I was going to say, I always thought that was a little too slow money for me. I, I, well I should have because there wasn't nothing to it, you know. Most of the guys got in just for the money of it, you see. But like I say, then I was doing a little range, I was selling arrangements around you and everything, you know. But I, I, in other words, I was doing it just as good as those guys there, you see. So, and then another thing I, I didn't like it because the time that, like, you would get a good job, it would be time to play with the WPA band, you see. That's the way I had to figure it out, you see. So, like I say, I was living there and then, that time Sidney, I don't know, him and I got in, got in a humble about something, I don't know. And he was dicking around with Randy, which, you know, like I say, you're going around, you hear a different thing. Well, Randy and I was good friends, we never was him or that. So, after I found out he was going to really let me go. So, I just said, well, and they found he did let me go and I found out he had Randy rehearsed. He wasn't calling me for rehearsal, you know. That's the way guys did. They wouldn't come out and tell you to just call another man, you see. Well, he figured you'd hear about it. So, I found out, I said, well, ain't nothing to it. I said, what you all do, miss that little money. So, alright, so one day I was sitting on my step and a fellow named Leo Dejon, he came to my house and he said, Sayers, I had been quiet about you, I heard you wasn't with Sidney. He said, you know, Peter Owen is organizing a band. He said, you know, we were, I'm with, he was working with a band called The Sunny South. And Peter Owen was kind of breaking up his old band. And Charlie and the two other brothers had a little job somewhere else and Steve was working somewhere else, you know. So, you know, I've been given this second, what do you call it, second band work all the time. Even when he was heading to the old band, you see. So, it was something, I don't know whatever came about, it looked like he was trying to break away from them. So, Leo said, how about coming around in rehearsal? So, they was having rehearsal at a fellow named Alec Grutterhouse on, on Iber, that's BN, brother. And then, I remember, in the band, between, let's see, the second block on the other side of Claiborne, that's, anyhow, his dad had a, by the place, Cornelia called me, they had a chup, a chupapain place, old man Alec Grutterhouse. And he, his wife was there and he was raising his daughter and his son, his son was Alec Grutterhouse. So, we used to rehearse around there and that band, when I got in the band, I went to rehearsal at first there, they had, uh, Peter Arn was just the leader. In the brass section they had the Leo Deja on trumpet, Joe Fuller on second trumpet, he had, I learned he had just got with him. And they had Eddie Pearson on trombone. And the sax section was Joe Ruzon on tenor, Arthur Durbny on first alto, and Elliot Taylor on third or either fourth, they used to swap around. And the rhythm section was me on, I was playing banjo and guitar in those days, on banjo and guitar. Alfred William on drum, Simon Moreira on bass and Alec Grutter on piano. And Alec Grutter was doing most of the arrangement, see, because he had a lot of history. Who was the leader? That was Peter on band, second. That was his, that was his. Wait, Violin rhythm? Yeah, he was the leader of the band. His band. On a drummer? You had a drummer?
Well, Alfred William on drum.

Yeah, I didn't get that. Alfred William on drum. drums. So Peter Hone had nice work like the field work like it is now playing like at the New Orleans Country Club. He had that tied up. Anything that was out there, he was a house band because they had a man named Mr. Crawford Ellis. That's the man that's got interest in Boat Young, a little bit around the South American and the Pan American insurance. And he liked the Peter Hone band. And then we had work like at the metric club and then we had work like out the Ottoman Park and we used to play for those like the kids, what you call them, we call them the frat house with plenty of houses. And then Peter Hone had a nice connection with like I know of the autocrat clubs. And at the time they had something they would hire his band and they liked it, what he called his second band, which is really his, because he had put the first band down, you see, because it was a regular ten piece band. Then he had a fellow named Harry Wells sing. Harry Wells was like a fellow like I'd call Earl Williams today. He could sing London songs fast, he could sing pop tunes and he could sing blues and everything and he could pick up on the song right away, you see, because we could come there with music and we'd play once or twice and he had it. That was during the Depression. Oh, that's during the Depression. So we, uh, that was about, I can say about the year, about the year of 30, 32 or 33. I was living on Prairie in La Hampa. Yeah, yeah. So Gene, he stayed with Sidney and Sidney, Sidney had the job on the boat then I believe, because Sidney had the job on the boat and I first left there. I stood, that was 1930 I remember. We had played that, because that was the first time we had played, the boat had been up to St. Paul in many years and that was, that was a terrific day. But he had gotten background back by 33 or 34. Well anyhow, I stayed with you on band.
Mm-hm.

segments.title: Spelling of Sayles's name and where the family is listed
segments.summary: Sayles gives his full name, Emanuel Renne Sayles, pronounced 'Sales', and explains the family listing in the phone book under his late father George and his brothers.

segments.title: Father's Silver Leaf string band and the Claiborne Williams band in Donaldsonville
segments.summary: His father George played guitar in the Silver Leaf string band in the Irish Channel until his children came; his mother came from Donaldsonville, home of Claiborne Williams's reading brass band, which Sayles remembers playing Sunday concerts.

segments.title: Looking at photographs of Donaldsonville streets and buildings
segments.summary: The interviewer shows pictures of Donaldsonville and Sayles identifies Railroad Avenue, the market and the Bank of Ascension.

segments.title: Childhood in Donaldsonville: first school and father's hotel work
segments.summary: He recalls his first school, the family's Donaldsonville home, the move around 1915, and his father's hard jobs and night-desk work at the hotel, plus playing now and then with a second local band.

segments.title: Father's stories about Joe Oliver working on the riverfront
segments.summary: His father knew Joe Oliver, who lived on Fort Street c. 1915, worked on the riverfront for white employers who let him play weekends, and bought his first cornet that way.

segments.title: Country musicians who came to New Orleans: Humphrey, Robichaud, Celestin
segments.summary: He recalls his father's accounts of old man Humphrey teaching in the country and of musicians such as John Robichaud and Celestin coming to the city from rural places to find work.

segments.title: Richard M. Jones, Dave Perkins, his father's friends and cousin Peter Raphael
segments.summary: Asked about Donaldsonville-area musicians, he names Jones, Porter, Dave Perkins as a teacher of white and colored pupils, and his father's friends, then explains that Aunt Bella is the mother of drummer Peter Raphael, his first cousin.

segments.title: Father's death and burial in Hope Cemetery
segments.summary: Sayles gives his father's name, Joy (George) Sayles, and recalls his death and burial with his mother and sister in Hope Cemetery.

segments.title: Claiborne Williams as teacher and his brother George's fatal illness
segments.summary: He compares Claiborne Williams to Dave Perkins as a teacher of both races, and tells his father's story of Claiborne's travelling brother George, a trombonist who died after a pneumonia while Claiborne nursed him.

segments.title: Funerals, baptisms and brass bands in Donaldsonville compared with New Orleans
segments.summary: Donaldsonville funerals had brass bands but less second line than New Orleans; he describes baptism processions with humming to the river and the family's move around 1915.

segments.title: Birth date in 1907 and a photograph of the Donaldsonville church
segments.summary: He gives his birth date as January 31, 1907, his baptism in a church shared by both races, and identifies the church in a picture.

segments.title: The big storm, his grandfather, and his great-aunt who read French
segments.summary: He recalls his grandfather's account of storm damage in New Orleans, relatives living in the city, and his French-reading seamstress great-aunt.

segments.title: Move to New Orleans and bands advertising at the corner saloon
segments.summary: The family moves to the corner of Oak and Bordeaux (c. 1915-16); bands stop at the saloon to advertise dances, and young Sayles bangs on tin and wants to play jazz.

segments.chapter: Learning violin and banjo in New Orleans
segments.title: Father teaches him guitar chords and arranges violin lessons with Dave Perkins
segments.summary: His father tests his sons with chord shapes, teaches Emanuel guitar changes, decides he should play violin, and buys a viola for $10 so he can study with his friend Dave Perkins.

segments.chapter: Learning violin and banjo in New Orleans
segments.title: Violin method with Dave Perkins and picking up banjo with Morris and Mack
segments.summary: Perkins starts him on rudiments and the fingerboard for three years; his brother's banjo leads him to read and fake with George Morris and others, and he graduates eighth grade.

segments.chapter: Learning violin and banjo in New Orleans
segments.title: Rampart Street dance halls: Bulls Club, San Souci Hall and neighbourhood bands
segments.summary: His father takes him to hear bands at the Bulls Club and San Souci Hall; he recalls Kid Rena's band, Jack Carey's band, Zutty Singleton, torchlight parades and Holy Ghost church dances.

segments.chapter: Learning violin and banjo in New Orleans
segments.title: Looking at a record cover photograph: Jack Carey, Punch and Edmund Hall
segments.summary: A bystander says he played with Jack Carey, and the group looks at a Savoy album picture identifying Punch and Edmund Hall.

segments.chapter: Learning violin and banjo in New Orleans
segments.title: Switching to banjo and rehearsing with George Morris, Thomas Mack and Edmund Washington
segments.summary: Sayles explains how he took over his brother's banjo while his friends, all pupils of Dave Perkins, had trumpet, trombone and clarinet lessons and rehearsed together.

segments.chapter: Learning violin and banjo in New Orleans
segments.title: Early jobs in Polyland and on the riverfront, then leaving for Pensacola with Joe Wynn
segments.summary: The young band plays a rough Prohibition-era place in Polyland and a foundry office during a strike, then in April 1924 Joe Wynn recruits them for Pensacola despite his mother's objections, leaving cousin Pete behind.

segments.title: Arriving in Pensacola: Joe Wynn's backers and Prince Morris's rival band
segments.summary: Wynn broke from Prince Morris and teamed with a doctor and Aaron Long, who ran Morris Park; Sayles finds Lee Collins's band there and Wynn lures Edmund Hall and Albert Morgan into the New Orleans group.

segments.title: Pensacola pianists and who played in Prince Morris's band and Wynn's band
segments.summary: Questions about the Goodson sisters from Pensacola lead to a lineup of Prince Morris's group with Lee Collins and a recollection of how Wynn assembled the visiting band.

segments.title: Edmund Hall and Edmund Washington sharing the sax and clarinet parts
segments.summary: Hall could not read well, so Washington played lead and Hall learned it by ear, while Hall was the better jazz clarinetist and Washington the better saxophonist.

segments.title: C-melody sax, 'Christine' and playing the Pensacola ballpark pavilion
segments.summary: Hall played a C-melody and copied the record 'Christine'; the band played an open-air pavilion with advertising before dances and battles with rival bands.

segments.title: Mobile, the 'Pensacola Jazz' name, nearby towns and radio broadcasts
segments.summary: The band is unnamed until a big night at Brooklyn Park in Mobile wins them the name Pensacola Jazz; they play Alabama and Florida towns, the radio station and a hotel.

segments.title: How fast New Orleans bands played for dancers in the 1920s
segments.summary: Sayles explains that New Orleans dancers wanted moderate tempos for dancing and talking, and that faster tempos came later with college crowds and Lindy hop.

segments.title: Tiger Rag and the Jack Carey name
segments.summary: He says the tune called 'Jack Carey' was really Tiger Rag, which the leader would call out during the number.

segments.title: Mobile's Excelsior Brass Band, Cootie Williams and the New Orleans beat
segments.summary: Tiger Rag was the fastest tune; he describes the Excelsior band under Johnny Pope, the union's resistance to outsiders, Cootie Williams copying Sam Morgan and Punch, and the Gomez auditorium hiring New Orleans bands.

segments.title: Growl trumpet and mutes: derby, glass and bottle; Chris Kelly
segments.summary: Cootie growled by hand, derby or glass; Sayles and a trumpeter visitor swap talk of aluminium mutes, Chris Kelly's blues on a derby, and improvised mutes.

segments.title: Trumpeter leaves; resuming the Pensacola story
segments.summary: The visitor says goodbye and the interviewer asks Sayles to go back to the Pensacola band.

segments.title: Aaron Long books a trip to Jacksonville and Eagle Eye blocks them
segments.summary: Aaron Long gives up his market to book the band to Jacksonville, hoping for Tampa and Miami, but Eagle Eye's band keeps them out of the Elks Hall.

segments.title: Joe Wynn skips town, Pete Raphael joins, and the vote not to go farther into Florida
segments.summary: Wynn disappears over money trouble, Chinee Foster and then cousin Pete drum, the Jacksonville dance goes badly then wins crowds, and the band votes to return, a decision Sayles calls a mistake.

segments.chapter: The Pelican band and Ridgley years
segments.title: Pensacola band breaks up and Sayles returns to join Bebe Ridgley's Pelican band
segments.summary: Eagle Eye hires Edmund Hall away, Albert Morgan goes home with Sam Morgan, Sayles returns to New Orleans c. 1927 and joins Ridgley's Pelican Roof band with David Jones directing.

segments.chapter: The Pelican band and Ridgley years
segments.title: Celestin's band personnel and drummers like Snaggs
segments.summary: Questions about Emma Barron and Celestin's lineup with Polo Barnes lead to a discussion of the drummers of that time, including eccentric show drummer Snaggs.

segments.chapter: The Pelican band and Ridgley years
segments.title: The Pelican hall and the rivalry with the Roof Garden, Astoria and Fate Marable
segments.summary: He describes the upstairs Pelican, the four competing dance halls, the contest of two-, three- and four-band nights, and Marable's boat band playing late after the boat closed.

segments.chapter: The Pelican band and Ridgley years
segments.title: Bud Scott, Natchez excursion bands and the cup contest with Claiborne Williams
segments.summary: Bud Scott was the Natchez singer-leader whose band came on excursions, and the Pelican band faced Claiborne Williams's Donaldsonville band in a trophy-cup contest.

segments.chapter: The Pelican band and Ridgley years
segments.title: One Eye Babe's gut bucket band, Sam Red Allen and fingerpicked guitar
segments.summary: Small gut-bucket bands played at the Pelican with One Eye Babe on bass and his son on banjo, and Sayles remembers a guitarist who played blues with his fingers.

segments.chapter: The Pelican band and Ridgley years
segments.title: Fingerstyle guitar: his father's technique and Guitar Slim today
segments.summary: His father played a six-string guitar without a pick or thumb pick; Sayles says Guitar Slim and others now play rock and roll and blues with fingers.

segments.chapter: The Pelican band and Ridgley years
segments.title: Guitar-banjo and tenor banjo tunings in the old bands
segments.summary: Early banjoists such as Johnny St. Cyr and Lorenzo Starr used a banjo-guitar before the tenor banjo became popular; he also notes the Pelican band's fame, and Ridgley's move toward Suburban Garden.

segments.chapter: The Pelican band and Ridgley years
segments.title: Suburban Garden in Jefferson Parish and Jack Sheen the Coconut King
segments.summary: Sayles and Ridgley open Jack Sheen's new gambling club near the levee until police raids close it, and the interviewer checks what instrument Ridgley played.

segments.title: Sitting in at the entertainment club and replacing Willie Foster with Fate Marable
segments.summary: Musicians gather at an entertainment club; Marable, hearing him and urged by trumpeter Albert Snyder and his brother who works the boat, auditions him and hires him on banjo.

segments.title: Lineup of Fate Marable's boat band
segments.summary: Sayles names the reeds, brass and rhythm players of the Marable band on the boat, including Norman Mason, Albert Snyder, Nat Story and Lewis Eckerhardt.

segments.title: The St. Louis season, meeting his first wife Alma, and being let go in Memphis
segments.summary: He plays the New Orleans and St. Louis seasons, Captain Joe coaches him to sing, he meets Alma, and is told 'the axe is on you' as Red returns, with a bonus and pay from the Streckfus company.

segments.title: Timing programs and tempos on the Streckfus excursion boats
segments.summary: The company timed each program so many numbers fit, with leaders keeping precise tempos and faster Lindy hop tempos required in St. Louis.

segments.title: Beale Street in Memphis and returning to New Orleans with Ridgley
segments.summary: After being fired he stays in Memphis, walks Beale Street, drinks with Red, then returns home and rejoins Ridgley's band, meeting young trumpeter Gilbert Young.

segments.title: Jitney dance halls and the Astoria band with Lee Collins and David Jones
segments.summary: He takes John Marrero's banjo job at the La Vila jitney dance hall, then joins Lee Collins, David Jones and John Robichaud at the Astoria, where Albert Morgan joins on bass and Don Albert arrives.

segments.title: The Astoria floor show and advertising by truck on Rampart Street
segments.summary: Sherman Cook emceed a floor show for mixed audiences, and the band advertised from a truck and balcony on Rampart Street.

segments.title: Recording 'Astoria Strut' and 'Damp Weather Blues' with Sidney Arodin
segments.summary: At the old Italian Hall they record with Sidney Arodin on clarinet, struggling with the drummer and bass, and the tunes are built on Sister Kate changes with the blues title coming from a rainy day.

segments.title: Who scatted on the record and a later Chicago reunion with Albert Morgan
segments.summary: Albert Morgan did the scat vocal; Sayles recalls meeting him in Chicago, and Don Albert starts raiding local bands for his new group.

segments.chapter: Desvigne, Chicago offers and Peter Hone's band
segments.title: Don Albert's offer versus the Desvigne boat job
segments.summary: Albert tries to hire him for his new band, but Sayles, sick and short of money, takes a salaried boat season with Sidney Desvigne.

segments.chapter: Desvigne, Chicago offers and Peter Hone's band
segments.title: Danny Barker, the Chicago excursion and the offers Sayles turned down
segments.summary: He recommends Danny Barker for Albert's job, tells how Barker met his uncle Paul and went to Chicago, calls it a missed break, then returns to Desvigne's band living near Randy Hall.

segments.chapter: Desvigne, Chicago offers and Peter Hone's band
segments.title: Declining the WPA band, losing Desvigne's job, and joining Peter Hone's second band
segments.summary: He finds the WPA band too slow-paying, learns Desvigne has replaced him, and Leo Dejan recruits him for Peter Hone's band, whose personnel he lists.

segments.chapter: Desvigne, Chicago offers and Peter Hone's band
segments.title: Peter Hone's society-circuit jobs and singer Harry Wells during the Depression
segments.summary: Hone's band holds country club and fraternity work and uses singer Harry Wells, in the Depression years around 1930-33.
